title: Frequency-Uniform Log-Regret Reinforcement Learning for Diffusions

paper.title:
Frequency-Uniform Log-Regret Reinforcement Learning
for Diffusions
paper.abstract:
Abstract High-frequency control problems are often studied through time discretization, but refining the timestep δ \delta increases the discrete
horizon H = T / δ H=T/\delta and can make standard finite-horizon regret guarantees
deteriorate even when the physical horizon T T is fixed. We study episodic
value-based reinforcement learning for Euler discretizations of controlled
diffusions. The performance is measured as the cumulative regret over K K episodes relative to the
optimal policy of the corresponding Euler model.
Under stability and regularity conditions on value function gradients, Bellman residual derivatives,
and fitted critics, we prove an 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ K ) \mathcal{O}(\log K) regret bound with constants uniform in δ \delta .
For dynamics with drift linear in
unknown parameters and unknown constant diffusion covariance, we verify
localized versions of these conditions for a constrained, model-based
controlled-diffusion fitted- Q Q algorithm (CD-FQ) and obtain high-probability 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ K ​ log ⁡ log ​ K ) \mathcal{O}(\log K\log\log K) regret for fixed and finite T T , again with constants uniform in δ \delta .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: A learning guarantee for a stochastic control system should distinguish between how long the system operates and how often its decisions are updated. In a service system controlled over a fixed planning period, halving the time between interventions doubles the number of decision stages but leaves the physical duration unchanged. A regret bound polynomial in the stage count can therefore predict an arbitrarily large learning cost as the decision grid is refined. This sensitivity matters when choosing how frequently to observe, learn, and act: it obscures whether a performance guarantee reflects the difficulty of controlling the system or the temporal resolution used to describe it. Our objective is to identify conditions under which value-based reinforcement learning retains fast regret guarantees as that resolution increases. Sequential decision problems arise throughout science and engineering whenever present actions affect the uncertain evolution of a system. Examples include treatment planning ( Wang et al. 2024 ) , robotic control ( Djeumou et al. 2023 ) , inventory ( Dai and Yao 2013 ) , service operations ( Ward and Kumar 2008 ) , and financial decisions ( Pham 2009 ) . Reinforcement learning for queueing networks ( Dai and Gluzman 2022 ) and optimal execution in financial markets ( Wang et al. 2026a ) illustrate the value of exploiting the structure of the underlying stochastic dynamics in the context of learning. This perspective motivates our focus on controlled diffusions, which provide tractable approximations of complex operational systems by capturing the aggregate effects of their random events ( Harrison and Van Mieghem 1997 , Braverman et al. 2020 ) . These models also provide a foundation for stochastic control ( Ata et al. 2026 ) and continuous-time reinforcement learning ( Wang et al. 2020 ) . We study episodic value-based learning for Euler discretizations of controlled diffusions in continuous state and action spaces. Over a fixed physical horizon T T , a timestep δ \delta produces H = T / δ H=T/\delta decision stages per episode. The learner uses data from previous episodes to select policies and is evaluated by cumulative conditional expected regret relative to the optimal policy of the same Euler model. Existing finite-horizon analyses can achieve logarithmic regret in the number of episodes while retaining polynomial dependence on H H . For example, the leading fast-rate term in the online fitted- Q Q guarantee of Duan and Wainwright (2024) contains an H 4 H^{4} factor. Substituting H = T / δ H=T/\delta gives a polynomial penalty in 1 / δ 1/\delta at fixed T T , because it tracks only the number of stages and not how one-step rewards and state increments scale with the timestep. This raises a distinct question: How can we design online learning algorithms that retain fast rate and log regret as the observation and decision frequency increases? The question is particularly delicate for value-based learning. Because an action is held for only one timestep, its effect on the one-step value and the action-dependent differences in the ordinary Q Q -function are of order δ \delta . Learning must therefore resolve a shrinking action signal while controlling error propagation across T / δ T/\delta stages, and keep the deployed policies informative. This scaling also motivates advantage-rate representations and continuous-time q q -learning ( Tallec et al. 2019 , Jia and Zhou 2023 ) .

sections.heading: 1.1 Our work and contributions
sections.text: We develop a regret framework that guides the design and analysis of a fitted-Q algorithm.

sections.heading: A discrete-to-continuous fast-regret framework.
sections.text: We formulate episodic value-based learning for a family of Euler models indexed by the timestep δ \delta , separating episode count, physical horizon, and decision frequency, and placing discrete-time regret analysis and diffusion control in a common framework. The benchmark is the optimum of the corresponding Euler model, so statistical learning regret remains distinct from continuous-time discretization error ( Section 2 ). Our bounds concern statistical performance at fixed physical horizon; the number of observations and the computational effort can still grow as the grid is refined.

sections.heading: Discretization-uniform logarithmic regret.
sections.text: We formulate criteria on fitted critics that are sufficient for fast regret, separating the policy-performance argument from algorithm-specific verification ( Criteria 1 and 2a ). Under quadratic advantage and value-gradient stability conditions, Bellman-residual derivatives of order δ / k \delta/\sqrt{k} after k k episodes yield critic action-gradient errors of the same order, with constants governed by physical time. Quadratic policy loss then gives 𝒪 ⁡ ( δ / k ) ​ action-gradient error ⟹ 𝒪 ⁡ ( δ / k ) ​ loss per stage ⟹ 𝒪 ⁡ ( T / k ) ​ loss per episode . \displaystyle\mathcal{O}(\delta/\sqrt{k})\,\,\textrm{action-gradient error}\Longrightarrow\mathcal{O}(\delta/k)\,\,\textrm{loss per stage}\Longrightarrow\mathcal{O}(T/k)\,\,\textrm{loss per episode}. Summing over episodes gives 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ K ) \mathcal{O}(\log K) regret for fixed T T , with constants uniform in δ \delta ( Theorem 2.7 ). An explicit fitted-critic construction shows that exponential growth in T T of the logarithmic-regret coefficient is unavoidable for a guarantee uniform over this general class ( Proposition 2.10 ).

sections.heading: End-to-end learning to verify 𝒪 ~ ​ ( log ⁡ K ) \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\log K) regret.
sections.text: For controlled diffusions with drift linear in unknown parameters and unknown constant diffusion covariance, we develop a constrained, model-based fitted- Q Q algorithm (CD-FQ) that permits finitely many separated optimal branch points. It estimates the drift parameter by projected least squares and the covariance from residual increments, simulates from the fitted Euler model, fits constrained critics backward from the terminal reward (a discrete analogue of solving the HJB equation), and chooses a policy greedily. Under regularity, exploration, approximation, and simulation-budget conditions, it achieves high-probability 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ K ​ log ⁡ log ​ K ) \mathcal{O}(\log K\log\log K) regret with constants uniform in δ \delta ( Theorem 3.5 ). The analysis jointly establishes critic accuracy and the continued self-exploration property of the greedy policies.

sections.heading: Verification and numerical evidence.
sections.text: A model with two optimal branches jointly verifies all assumptions of the learning theorem ( Section 5.1 ). Queueing experiments examine cumulative regret, stability under timestep refinement, and transfer of learned diffusion policies to finite many-server queues ( Section 5.2 ). These experiments extend beyond the theorem’s smoothness, boundedness, and action-space assumptions and assess the practical value of exploiting diffusion structure.

sections.heading: Stability and fast rates in discrete-time RL.
sections.text: The closest fast-rate analyses are Duan and Wainwright (2024) and Wang et al. (2026b) . Duan and Wainwright (2024) obtain quadratic performance bounds and fast offline and online rates through Bellman and occupation-measure stability. Wang et al. (2026b) study value-based RL in discounted stochastic control with continuous actions. They prove an 𝒪 ⁡ ( n − 1 ) \mathcal{O}(n^{-1}) expected policy gap for the deployed policy, where n n indexes estimator accuracy and may represent sample size, but without an end-to-end online algorithm. Our analysis shares a related quadratic error-to-loss mechanism and tracks how derivative bounds on stagewise Bellman residuals propagate through the finite-horizon recursion. Under the stated conditions, this gives logarithmic cumulative online regret with constants uniform in δ \delta at the fixed physical horizon T T . The regret bounds in Duan and Wainwright (2024) retain polynomial dependence on the number of decision stages H H , which does not by itself establish uniformity as δ \delta decreases at fixed T T . Our bound establishes this uniformity while having exponential dependence on T T , sharp under our assumptions ( Proposition 2.10 ).

sections.heading: Episodic learning in continuous time.
sections.text: The square-root regret bounds for jump processes in Gao and Zhou (2026) and fast rates for structured diffusions in Basei et al. (2022) , Szpruch et al. (2026) highlight the role of structure and information in continuous-time learning. In particular, Szpruch et al. (2026) distinguish explicit exploration from self-exploration, where greedy exploitation supplies informative data. Guo et al. (2023) analyze episodic learning for linear-convex jump-diffusions through stability of feedback controls, linking least-squares estimation error to sublinear regret. For exploratory finite-horizon linear-quadratic control, Giegrich et al. (2024) establish convergence of policy-gradient methods with guarantees that remain stable as the action frequency increases. We develop this mechanism for fitted critics with approximation error and multiple optimal branch points, extending the scope under different model and regularity assumptions.

sections.heading: Continuous-time q q -learning and function approximation.
sections.text: For deterministic policies, Cheng et al. (2025) derive a continuous-time policy gradient via an advantage-rate function, leading to a model-free algorithm stable across time discretizations. The exploratory-control framework of Wang et al. (2020) and continuous-time q q -learning of Jia and Zhou (2023) replace vanishing one-step action gaps with instantaneous advantages. Recent work establishes regret guarantees for exploratory policy improvement and q q -learning ( Tang and Zhou 2024 ) , as well as model-free, off-policy guarantees for value and advantage approximation ( Mou 2026 ) . We instead study cumulative online regret for deterministic greedy fitted- Q Q policies and verify the required derivative accuracy for a learned parametric diffusion.

sections.heading: Discretization and continuous-time approximation.
sections.text: A related line of work asks how well discrete-time procedures recover their continuous-time counterparts. Approximating continuous-time stochastic control by discrete models has a classical foundation in numerical stochastic control ( Kushner and Dupuis 2001 ) . PhiBE ( Zhu 2024 ) and the high-order Bellman schemes of Mou and Zhu (2026) evaluate policies from discretely observed diffusion trajectories, and Optimal-PhiBE ( Zhu et al. 2025 ) and PhiBE-Q-Learning ( Zhu and Ren 2026 ) carry this PDE-based approach over to policy optimization and off-policy learning. On the implementation side, Jia et al. (2026) quantify the error of executing a continuous-time stochastic policy by resampling actions on a grid, and Pham et al. (2026) bound the gap between regularized discrete-time Bellman problems and the underlying continuous-time control problem. In each case the quantity of interest is an approximation error, whether of a value function, policy, or execution scheme. We ask a different question: how much cumulative regret an online learner incurs against the Euler optimum at step size δ \delta , with bounds that hold uniformly in δ \delta .

sections.heading: Roadmap.
sections.text: The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 develops the residual-to-regret framework. Section 3 introduces our method and states its main regret guarantee, proved in Section 4 . Section 5 presents numerical experiments. The appendices provide supporting proofs and implementation details, with notation and constants summarized in Appendix F for ease of reference.

sections.heading: 2.2 Residual accuracy and regret transfer
sections.text: The performance estimate reduces regret control to bounding critic action-gradient errors at the selected actions. We bound these by derivatives of the Bellman residuals under the true kernel. The Euler structure and value-gradient stability control the backward propagation, independently of how the fitted critics were constructed.

sections.heading: 3 Localized learning: algorithm and main result
sections.text: Section 2 identifies sufficient benchmark properties and residual accuracy for fast regret. We now localize the mechanism for a concrete learning algorithm. With several separated optimal branches, the benchmark inequalities may hold only inside unknown bins. The learner still maximizes over the full action set, so the proof must establish that its fitted greedy actions lie in regions where the inequalities apply. The two-scale residual control in Criterion 2b addresses this requirement. A coarse action-residual bound establishes bin entry jointly with backward transfer. Sharper residual bounds inside the bins then give local gradient control and quadratic policy loss. The local geometry also bounds distance to the optimal-action set, which supports the coverage and self-exploration arguments across epochs. The algorithm does not use the unknown bins; they enter only in the analysis. Table 10 in Appendix F collects the notation and constants used here and in the proof.

sections.heading: 3.2 Estimation scheme and learning algorithm
sections.text: At the start of epoch j j , the learner checks empirical coverage. If it passes, the learner uses all previously collected real transitions to estimate the dynamics. It then generates fresh synthetic Bellman targets under the estimated kernel, fits the critics backward in time, and deploys the greedy policy for the rest of the epoch. If the check fails, it instead deploys the exploration policy and skips both fits. We specify the construction here, and prove finite-sample accuracy in Section 4.1 .

sections.heading: 4 Proof of the main theorem
sections.text: Fix ( K , δ ) (K,\delta) and the assumptions of Theorem 3.5 . The proof closes a loop over epochs: empirical coverage at the epoch boundary n j n_{j} gives Criteria 1 and 2b at epoch j j ; these criteria give bin entry and local gradient control for π ( j ) \pi^{(j)} ; and the resulting proximity of π ( j ) \pi^{(j)} to the optimal-action sets implies coverage at the next fitted boundary n j + 1 n_{j+1} , when n j + 1 < K n_{j+1}<K . Section 4.1 verifies the two criteria on a simultaneous deviation event; Section 4.2 derives, deterministically for one epoch, bin entry, local gradient control, and proximity to the optimal-action set; Section 4.3 closes the loop by forward induction over epochs; and Section 4.4 sums the one-episode losses over epochs. Concentration arguments are in Appendix B and detailed proofs and threshold calculations in Appendix C . The residual, transfer, and threshold constants are summarized in Table 10 .

Final learning regret at K = 8192 K=8192 ranges from 0.0136 0.0136 to 0.0168 0.0168 across H H , and all pairwise bootstrap intervals contain zero, so it shows no detectable change across the sixteenfold grid refinement. Exploration regret approaches an extrapolated limit of 0.0170 0.0170 at approximately first order in δ \delta , reflecting convergence of the Euler benchmark. Cumulative regret grows approximately linearly in log ⁡ K \log K ( Section D.5 ). sections.heading: 5.2 Halfin–Whitt queueing example
sections.text: We next study service-speed control in a many-server queue under Halfin–Whitt scaling ( Halfin and Whitt 1981 ) . To assess the framework’s learning efficiency and robustness, we examine cumulative regret, stability under timestep refinement, performance relative to two value-based baselines, and transferrability of Euler-trained policies to finite queues.

sections.heading: 5.2.1 Experimental setup
sections.text: The state is the diffusion-scaled number of customers relative to the number of servers, and the action increases service speed. With x + = max ⁡ { x , 0 } x^{+}=\max\{x,0\} and x − = max ⁡ { − x , 0 } x^{-}=\max\{-x,0\} , training uses the Euler model X h + 1 = X h + δ ⁡ ( − β + μ ​ X h − − κ ​ A h ) + 2 ​ μ ​ δ ​ ε h , ε h ​ ∼ iid ​ N ​ ( 0 , 1 ) , X_{h+1}=X_{h}+\delta(-\beta+\mu X_{h}^{-}-\kappa A_{h})+\sqrt{2\mu\delta}\,\varepsilon_{h},\qquad\varepsilon_{h}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,1), (73) over H = T / δ H=T/\delta stages, with T = 5 T=5 , X 0 = 0 X_{0}=0 , μ = 1 \mu=1 , β = 1 / 2 \beta=1/2 , and κ = 1 \kappa=1 . We minimize J δ ​ ( π ) = 𝔼 π ​ ∑ h = 0 H − 1 δ ​ ℓ ​ ( X h , A h ) J_{\delta}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}\delta\ell(X_{h},A_{h}) , where ℓ ⁡ ( x , a ) = q ​ x + + c ​ a 2 / 2 \ell(x,a)=qx^{+}+ca^{2}/2 and q = c = 1 q=c=1 , with zero terminal cost. In the reward convention of Section 2 , r = − ℓ r=-\ell . Actions lie on 𝒜 0.25 = { 0 , 0.25 , … , 2 } \mathcal{A}_{0.25}=\{0,0.25,\ldots,2\} . Our learner, controlled-diffusion fitted- Q Q ( CD-FQ ), estimates ( β , κ ) (\beta,\kappa) and the diffusion variance from fixed-stage observations, retaining the known drift term μ ​ x − \mu x^{-} . After initial exploration (64 episodes in Experiments 1(a)–1(b), and 32 in 2(a)–2(b)), it fits constrained cubic-spline critics using fresh Gaussian next-state samples from the estimated model and updates the greedy policy at dyadic episode counts. Numerical parameters are fixed across timesteps within each study. For the policy π k \pi_{k} deployed in episode k k , we measure R K = ∑ k = 1 K { J δ ​ ( π k ) − J δ ​ ( π δ ref ) } , R_{K}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\{J_{\delta}(\pi_{k})-J_{\delta}(\pi^{\mathrm{ref}}_{\delta})\}, (74) where π δ ref \pi^{\mathrm{ref}}_{\delta} is a numerical Euler reference on the same action grid and timestep, computed by dynamic programming using the true model parameters. Thus R K R_{K} is the regret ( 4 ) with J δ ⋆ J_{\delta}^{\star} replaced by J δ ​ ( π δ ref ) J_{\delta}(\pi^{\mathrm{ref}}_{\delta}) , and J δ ​ ( π ) − J δ ​ ( π δ ref ) J_{\delta}(\pi)-J_{\delta}(\pi^{\mathrm{ref}}_{\delta}) is the policy gap of π \pi . These are evaluated using 32,768 paired simulations episodes, with the learned and reference policies receiving identical Gaussian noise draws within each pair. Experiments 1(a) and 1(b) each use eight independent training seeds per timestep, with separate seed sets. Experiments 2(a) and 2(b) use 15 new matched seeds per timestep and a 512-episode budget; Experiment 2(b) transfers the policies from 2(a). Reported intervals are marginal 95% Student- t t intervals across the training seeds. Appendix E.1 gives the queue scaling, Appendix E.2 the implementation, and Appendix E.3 the reference solver and evaluation details. This model lies outside our theory: the action set is a finite grid, the cost q ​ x + qx^{+} is not C 1 C^{1} , and the known drift term μ ​ x − \mu x^{-} is unbounded and not C 1 C^{1} . The experiments are therefore a stress test of CD-FQ beyond the assumptions of Theorem 3.5 .

sections.heading: 5.2.4 Experiment 2(a): common-budget Euler learning
sections.text: We compare CD-FQ with two families of baselines at a common interaction budget. CD-FQ assumes the parametric controlled-diffusion form of ( 73 ), which the Euler training model satisfies exactly, and is given the known drift term μ ​ x − \mu x^{-} ; the baselines use neither. Experiment 2(b) tests whether the advantage persists when the learned policies are transferred to finite queues, which the diffusion only approximates. The first baseline is backward fitted- Q Q iteration following Duan and Wainwright (2024) (DW). Source-style DW fits only the newest epoch’s episodes at each refit. DW + replay pools all past episodes, including initial exploration, while re-using the other DW settings. The second family is a finite-action implementation of little- q q ( Jia and Zhou 2023 ) , which learns a value function and action score from martingale orthogonality conditions. Online little- q q updates after every episode; batch little- q q solves the conditions on all observed data at dyadic refits. The main comparison uses online little- q q ’s native Gibbs policy at temperature ν = 0.2 \nu=0.2 . Batch little- q q also uses ν = 0.2 \nu=0.2 and ridge coefficient ρ = 10 − 5 \rho=10^{-5} with a greedy policy for the terminal comparison (Appendix E.5 ). Every run receives the same type of fixed-stage tuple ( X h , A h , δ ​ ℓ ​ ( X h , A h ) , X h + 1 ) (X_{h},A_{h},\delta\ell(X_{h},A_{h}),X_{h+1}) on the same action grid, K = 512 K=512 episodes, and n 0 = 32 n_{0}=32 initial exploration episodes. The 15 seed labels are matched across methods and timesteps, though trajectories can differ when actions differ. This gives K ​ T = 2560 KT=2560 units of physical interaction and 512 ​ H 512H observed transitions per run at each horizon. Here CD-FQ uses exactly zero coefficient ridge. Timings and solver diagnostics appear in Appendix E.6 . The primary endpoint is the terminal value gap: the expected cost of the policy fitted after episode 512 minus that of the matched numerical Euler reference. It is estimated on the Euler model using paired simulation paths. Each reported interval is a marginal 95% Student- t t interval across the 15 independent training seeds. Statistical estimation error from finite randomized training samples and Monte Carlo error from the finite evaluation samples are not estimated separately. sections.heading: CD-FQ has the smallest terminal value gap.
sections.text: Its mean gap is 0.12 0.12 – 0.21 % 0.21\% of the reference cost across the four timesteps (Table 2 ). Replay reduces source-style DW’s mean gap by 45–73%, but its Euler gap exceeds online little- q q ’s at every tested timestep. Batch little- q q has the smallest mean gap among the baselines, but it is still about 24 24 – 26 % 26\% of the reference cost and 125–195 times CD-FQ ’s gap.

sections.heading: Coverage under the instantiated exploration schedule.
sections.text: All methods receive the same 32 uniform-action exploration episodes. Thereafter CD-FQ deploys greedy policies; its smallest saved information-matrix eigenvalue is 0.1104 0.1104 , above the coverage threshold 0.025 0.025 . This diagnostic concerns its cumulative design, including the initial exploration data. The online construction of Duan and Wainwright (2024, Section 3.2 and footnote 6) also uses an exploratory burn-in followed by greedy deployment and blockwise FQI refits on the newest epoch. It is presented as a conceptual consequence of their stability framework rather than as a fully specified practical algorithm. Our source-style DW instantiates this using the common 32-episode prefix. DW + replay retains the prefix observations and improves performance without additional exploration. Accordingly, the comparison characterize our finite-budget instantiation and its data-reuse choices, not the source paper’s general stability framework or its conditional guarantee.

sections.heading: The DW gaps increase under finer discretization.
sections.text: As δ \delta decreases from 0.2 0.2 to 0.025 0.025 , the source-style DW mean gap increases from 2.2811 2.2811 to 3.1641 3.1641 , and replay’s from 0.6229 0.6229 to 1.7441 1.7441 . CD-FQ ’s gap has no upward trend, while batch little- q q ’s greedy gap remains between 0.3211 0.3211 and 0.3642 0.3642 . Online little- q q ’s gap rises modestly, from 0.6098 0.6098 to 0.6575 0.6575 , but its policy remains close to initialization (Appendix E.6 ). These observations are consistent with the difficulty of regressing the ordinary Q Q -function’s 𝒪 ⁡ ( δ ) \mathcal{O}(\delta) action signal through T / δ T/\delta stages. They do not isolate that mechanism from differences in model knowledge, function approximation, regularization, or computation.

This measure includes the common exploration phase. It equals R 512 R_{512} in ( 74 ) plus mean-zero episode sampling noise and an offset between the reference policy’s expected cost and the numerical Bellman value, so its mean across runs estimates 𝔼 ⁡ [ R 512 ] \mathbb{E}[R_{512}] . CD-FQ ’s mean excess is 91.24 91.24 – 101.93 101.93 , versus 558.51 558.51 – 1254.88 1254.88 for replay. All primary comparator-minus- CD-FQ paired intervals are positive. Removing the shared exploration prefix leaves CD-FQ with mean realized excess 10.04 10.04 – 19.46 19.46 over 480 episodes.

sections.heading: CD-FQ transfers to finite queues best.
sections.text: Its mean queue gap is 0.0018 0.0018 – 0.0049 0.0049 , the smallest in all 12 configurations (Table 3 ). Batch little- q q is the strongest comparator in every cell ( 0.314 0.314 – 0.360 0.360 ). Replay improves on source-style DW throughout. CD-FQ ’s mean queue gap decreases with n n at each timestep. At n = 1600 n=1600 , it is 0.0038 0.0038 versus the Euler gap 0.0029 0.0029 at δ = 0.2 \delta=0.2 , and 0.0018 0.0018 versus 0.0017 0.0017 at δ = 0.025 \delta=0.025 . These point estimates are consistent with a residual Euler discretization effect: the queue approaches the diffusion, whereas training uses its Euler discretization. They do not establish a convergence rate. sections.heading: CD-FQ balances congestion and effort.
sections.text: A separate customer-level simulation estimates scaled mean wait, delay probability, and effort (Table 4 ). Wait and delay are pooled ratios over admitted arrivals, with 95% seed-cluster delta-method intervals ( t 14 t_{14} ), marginal or paired within seed; customers still waiting at T T are served at zero effort, so effort cost accumulates only through T T . Source-style DW has shorter waits and lower delay probability than CD-FQ but uses 5.8 5.8 – 7.4 7.4 times the effort. Online little- q q uses 20–24% less effort but roughly doubles the scaled mean wait. Replay’s tradeoff depends on resolution: at δ = 0.025 \delta=0.025 it waits less than CD-FQ but at much greater effort. Batch little- q q has longer waits and higher delay probability in all 12 cells without saving effort ( 0.533 0.533 – 0.683 0.683 vs. 0.511 0.511 – 0.538 0.538 ). CD-FQ has the lowest physical cost throughout. Note that these results concern frozen-policy transfer.

sections.heading: E.3 Euler reference and evaluation protocol
sections.text: For each timestep, backward dynamic programming computes the Euler Bellman-grid value V δ grid V_{\delta}^{\rm grid} on x ∈ [ − 8 , 12 ] x\in[-8,12] with state spacing 0.02 0.02 and the nine actions in 𝒜 0.25 \mathcal{A}_{0.25} . Gaussian integration uses piecewise-linear value interpolation with linear extrapolation and a nine-standard-deviation tail truncation. The reference policy π δ ref \pi_{\delta}^{\rm ref} uses the action at the nearest state knot, so its deployed actions stay on the declared grid; it is a numerical benchmark, not a certified optimum over continuous states and actions. A resolution check over state spacings 0.02 0.02 , 0.01 0.01 , and 0.005 0.005 found a paired cost difference of − 1.2 × 10 − 5 ± 3.3 × 10 − 5 -1.2\times 10^{-5}\pm 3.3\times 10^{-5} between the coarsest and finest reference policies. This supports the resolution at the reported gap scale but does not certify all reference errors uniformly in δ \delta . Euler policy gaps use 32,768 evaluation paths with common Brownian increments for each learned policy and its matched reference. Experiments 1(a)–1(b) weight each deployed-policy gap by its epoch length; reusing gaps correlates Monte Carlo errors across cumulative checkpoints. Experiment 2(a) evaluates terminal policies this way but uses observed training costs for cumulative excess, without re-evaluating intermediate policies. For Experiment 1(b)’s terminal recommendations, per-run paired Monte Carlo standard errors range from 5.8 × 10 − 5 5.8\times 10^{-5} to 2.4 × 10 − 4 2.4\times 10^{-4} . Experiments 1(a) and 1(b) use separate eight-seed cohorts, matched across timesteps within each cohort, and Student- t t intervals with seven degrees of freedom. Experiments 2(a)–2(b) share 15 prespecified seeds across methods and timesteps; all 60 timestep–seed runs per method are included, with two-sided 95% Student- t t intervals using 14 degrees of freedom. Paired intervals use within-seed comparator-minus- CD-FQ differences. Independent training seeds are the replicates; timesteps, episodes, and evaluation paths are not treated as independent training replicates. Intervals are marginal and unadjusted for multiple comparisons; they include Euler evaluation noise but do not propagate reference-solver bias. Numerical settings are selected on separate development seeds and fixed across timesteps within each study. Comparison methods share exogenous training streams and the 32-episode exploration prefix; subsequent trajectories can differ with their actions.

Emails: {jose.blanchet; lhao; renyuanxu}@stanford.edu . Authors are listed alphabetically. Lutong Hao 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Renyuan Xu 1 1 footnotemark: 1 October 26, 2026 Abstract High-frequency control problems are often studied through time discretization, but refining the timestep δ \delta increases the discrete horizon H = T / δ H=T/\delta and can make standard finite-horizon regret guarantees deteriorate even when the physical horizon T T is fixed. We study episodic value-based reinforcement learning for Euler discretizations of controlled diffusions. The performance is measured as the cumulative regret over K K episodes relative to the optimal policy of the corresponding Euler model. Under stability and regularity conditions on value function gradients, Bellman residual derivatives, and fitted critics, we prove an 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ K ) \mathcal{O}(\log K) regret bound with constants uniform in δ \delta . For dynamics with drift linear in unknown parameters and unknown constant diffusion covariance, we verify localized versions of these conditions for a constrained, model-based controlled-diffusion fitted- Q Q algorithm (CD-FQ) and obtain high-probability 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ K ​ log ⁡ log ​ K ) \mathcal{O}(\log K\log\log K) regret for fixed and finite T T , again with constants uniform in δ \delta . 1 Introduction A learning guarantee for a stochastic control system should distinguish between how long the system operates and how often its decisions are updated. In a service system controlled over a fixed planning period, halving the time between interventions doubles the number of decision stages but leaves the physical duration unchanged. A regret bound polynomial in the stage count can therefore predict an arbitrarily large learning cost as the decision grid is refined. This sensitivity matters when choosing how frequently to observe, learn, and act: it obscures whether a performance guarantee reflects the difficulty of controlling the system or the temporal resolution used to describe it. Our objective is to identify conditions under which value-based reinforcement learning retains fast regret guarantees as that resolution increases. Sequential decision problems arise throughout science and engineering whenever present actions affect the uncertain evolution of a system. Examples include treatment planning ( Wang et al. 2024 ) , robotic control ( Djeumou et al. 2023 ) , inventory ( Dai and Yao 2013 ) , service operations ( Ward and Kumar 2008 ) , and financial decisions ( Pham 2009 ) . Reinforcement learning for queueing networks ( Dai and Gluzman 2022 ) and optimal execution in financial markets ( Wang et al. 2026a ) illustrate the value of exploiting the structure of the underlying stochastic dynamics in the context of learning. This perspective motivates our focus on controlled diffusions, which provide tractable approximations of complex operational systems by capturing the aggregate effects of their random events ( Harrison and Van Mieghem 1997 , Braverman et al. 2020 ) . These models also provide a foundation for stochastic control ( Ata et al. 2026 ) and continuous-time reinforcement learning ( Wang et al. 2020 ) . We study episodic value-based learning for Euler discretizations of controlled diffusions in continuous state and action spaces. Over a fixed physical horizon T T , a timestep δ \delta produces H = T / δ H=T/\delta decision stages per episode. The learner uses data from previous episodes to select policies and is evaluated by cumulative conditional expected regret relative to the optimal policy of the same Euler model. Existing finite-horizon analyses can achieve logarithmic regret in the number of episodes while retaining polynomial dependence on H H . For example, the leading fast-rate term in the online fitted- Q Q guarantee of Duan and Wainwright (2024) contains an H 4 H^{4} factor. Substituting H = T / δ H=T/\delta gives a polynomial penalty in 1 / δ 1/\delta at fixed T T , because it tracks only the number of stages and not how one-step rewards and state increments scale with the timestep. This raises a distinct question: How can we design online learning algorithms that retain fast rate and log regret as the observation and decision frequency increases? The question is particularly delicate for value-based learning. Because an action is held for only one timestep, its effect on the one-step value and the action-dependent differences in the ordinary Q Q -function are of order δ \delta . Learning must therefore resolve a shrinking action signal while controlling error propagation across T / δ T/\delta stages, and keep the deployed policies informative. This scaling also motivates advantage-rate representations and continuous-time q q -learning ( Tallec et al. 2019 , Jia and Zhou 2023 ) . 1.1 Our work and contributions We develop a regret framework that guides the design and analysis of a fitted-Q algorithm. A discrete-to-continuous fast-regret framework. We formulate episodic value-based learning for a family of Euler models indexed by the timestep δ \delta , separating episode count, physical horizon, and decision frequency, and placing discrete-time regret analysis and diffusion control in a common framework. The benchmark is the optimum of the corresponding Euler model, so statistical learning regret remains distinct from continuous-time discretization error ( Section 2 ). Our bounds concern statistical performance at fixed physical horizon; the number of observations and the computational effort can still grow as the grid is refined. Discretization-uniform logarithmic regret. We formulate criteria on fitted critics that are sufficient for fast regret, separating the policy-performance argument from algorithm-specific verification ( Criteria 1 and 2a ). Under quadratic advantage and value-gradient stability conditions, Bellman-residual derivatives of order δ / k \delta/\sqrt{k} after k k episodes yield critic action-gradient errors of the same order, with constants governed by physical time. Quadratic policy loss then gives 𝒪 ⁡ ( δ / k ) ​ action-gradient error ⟹ 𝒪 ⁡ ( δ / k ) ​ loss per stage ⟹ 𝒪 ⁡ ( T / k ) ​ loss per episode . \displaystyle\mathcal{O}(\delta/\sqrt{k})\,\,\textrm{action-gradient error}\Longrightarrow\mathcal{O}(\delta/k)\,\,\textrm{loss per stage}\Longrightarrow\mathcal{O}(T/k)\,\,\textrm{loss per episode}. Summing over episodes gives 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ K ) \mathcal{O}(\log K) regret for fixed T T , with constants uniform in δ \delta ( Theorem 2.7 ). An explicit fitted-critic construction shows that exponential growth in T T of the logarithmic-regret coefficient is unavoidable for a guarantee uniform over this general class ( Proposition 2.10 ). End-to-end learning to verify 𝒪 ~ ​ ( log ⁡ K ) \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\log K) regret. For controlled diffusions with drift linear in unknown parameters and unknown constant diffusion covariance, we develop a constrained, model-based fitted- Q Q algorithm (CD-FQ) that permits finitely many separated optimal branch points. It estimates the drift parameter by projected least squares and the covariance from residual increments, simulates from the fitted Euler model, fits constrained critics backward from the terminal reward (a discrete analogue of solving the HJB equation), and chooses a policy greedily. Under regularity, exploration, approximation, and simulation-budget conditions, it achieves high-probability 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ K ​ log ⁡ log ​ K ) \mathcal{O}(\log K\log\log K) regret with constants uniform in δ \delta ( Theorem 3.5 ). The analysis jointly establishes critic accuracy and the continued self-exploration property of the greedy policies. Verification and numerical evidence. A model with two optimal branches jointly verifies all assumptions of the learning theorem ( Section 5.1 ). Queueing experiments examine cumulative regret, stability under timestep refinement, and transfer of learned diffusion policies to finite many-server queues ( Section 5.2 ). These experiments extend beyond the theorem’s smoothness, boundedness, and action-space assumptions and assess the practical value of exploiting diffusion structure. 1.2 Related work Stability and fast rates in discrete-time RL. The closest fast-rate analyses are Duan and Wainwright (2024) and Wang et al. (2026b) . Duan and Wainwright (2024) obtain quadratic performance bounds and fast offline and online rates through Bellman and occupation-measure stability. Wang et al. (2026b) study value-based RL in discounted stochastic control with continuous actions. They prove an 𝒪 ⁡ ( n − 1 ) \mathcal{O}(n^{-1}) expected policy gap for the deployed policy, where n n indexes estimator accuracy and may represent sample size, but without an end-to-end online algorithm. Our analysis shares a related quadratic error-to-loss mechanism and tracks how derivative bounds on stagewise Bellman residuals propagate through the finite-horizon recursion. Under the stated conditions, this gives logarithmic cumulative online regret with constants uniform in δ \delta at the fixed physical horizon T T . The regret bounds in Duan and Wainwright (2024) retain polynomial dependence on the number of decision stages H H , which does not by itself establish uniformity as δ \delta decreases at fixed T T . Our bound establishes this uniformity while having exponential dependence on T T , sharp under our assumptions ( Proposition 2.10 ). Episodic learning in continuous time. The square-root regret bounds for jump processes in Gao and Zhou (2026) and fast rates for structured diffusions in Basei et al. (2022) , Szpruch et al. (2026) highlight the role of structure and information in continuous-time learning. In particular, Szpruch et al. (2026) distinguish explicit exploration from self-exploration, where greedy exploitation supplies informative data. Guo et al. (2023) analyze episodic learning for linear-convex jump-diffusions through stability of feedback controls, linking least-squares estimation error to sublinear regret. For exploratory finite-horizon linear-quadratic control, Giegrich et al. (2024) establish convergence of policy-gradient methods with guarantees that remain stable as the action frequency increases. We develop this mechanism for fitted critics with approximation error and multiple optimal branch points, extending the scope under different model and regularity assumptions. Continuous-time q q -learning and function approximation. For deterministic policies, Cheng et al. (2025) derive a continuous-time policy gradient via an advantage-rate function, leading to a model-free algorithm stable across time discretizations. The exploratory-control framework of Wang et al. (2020) and continuous-time q q -learning of Jia and Zhou (2023) replace vanishing one-step action gaps with instantaneous advantages. Recent work establishes regret guarantees for exploratory policy improvement and q q -learning ( Tang and Zhou 2024 ) , as well as model-free, off-policy guarantees for value and advantage approximation ( Mou 2026 ) . We instead study cumulative online regret for deterministic greedy fitted- Q Q policies and verify the required derivative accuracy for a learned parametric diffusion. Discretization and continuous-time approximation. A related line of work asks how well discrete-time procedures recover their continuous-time counterparts. Approximating continuous-time stochastic control by discrete models has a classical foundation in numerical stochastic control ( Kushner and Dupuis 2001 ) . PhiBE ( Zhu 2024 ) and the high-order Bellman schemes of Mou and Zhu (2026) evaluate policies from discretely observed diffusion trajectories, and Optimal-PhiBE ( Zhu et al. 2025 ) and PhiBE-Q-Learning ( Zhu and Ren 2026 ) carry this PDE-based approach over to policy optimization and off-policy learning. On the implementation side, Jia et al. (2026) quantify the error of executing a continuous-time stochastic policy by resampling actions on a grid, and Pham et al. In each case the quantity of interest is an approximation error, whether of a value function, policy, or execution scheme.
